title: MATHEMATICAL METHODS
body:
The course where calculus stops being about one number in and one number out. [[CALCULUS 1]]
differentiated a curve, [[CALCULUS 2]] integrated one and then summed infinitely many terms, and
both worked with $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Here the input becomes a point and the output
often becomes a vector, and everything from the first two courses has to be rebuilt at that width:
a slope becomes a [[Gradient]], an integral becomes an integral over a region or along a path or
through a surface, and an equation relating a function to its derivatives becomes a
[[Partial Differential Equations|PDE]] describing a field varying in space and time.

Five blocks: [[Vector Calculus]], [[Multivariable Optimization|optimization in several variables]],
[[Differential Equations|systems of ODEs]], a rigorous revisit of convergence, and an introduction
to [[Partial Differential Equations|PDEs]]. Despite the ODE content the course is **not** a
differential equations course; vector calculus is the largest block and the one everything else
leans on.

**The single idea holding it together**: *the integral of a derivative over a region equals the
original object evaluated on that region's boundary.*
[[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus|The fundamental theorem of calculus]] said it for an interval
and its two endpoints. [[Green's Theorem]] says it for a plane region and its edge,
[[Stokes' Theorem]] for a surface and its rim, [[Divergence Theorem|the divergence theorem]]
for a solid and its skin. Learning them as four theorems is four times the work of learning
them as one.

For a CS degree this is where the maths behind machine learning actually lives.
[[Gradient Descent]] is [[Multivariable Optimization]] when there is no closed form,
[[Back Propagation]] is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] applied layer by layer, the Hessian of
[[Multivariable Optimization]] is the second-order test everyone approximates instead of computing,
and [[Principal Component Analysis]] is a [[Lagrange Multipliers]] problem whose multiplier turns
out to be an eigenvalue. It is also where [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]'s eigenvalues cash out in analysis:
[[Systems of Differential Equations]] is solved by [[Diagonalization]] and nothing else.

## Topics

### Multivariable differentiation

- [[Multivariable Calculus]]: the umbrella. One question, "what is the slope", splits into "the
  slope in which direction", and everything below is a consequence
- [[Partial Derivative]]: differentiate in one variable with the others held constant. No new
  technique, all new bookkeeping, and every operator in the course is built from these
- [[Gradient]]: the partials collected into a vector. Points along steepest ascent, is
  perpendicular to level sets, and dotted with a direction gives the rate of change that way
- [[Multivariable Chain Rule]]: a sum over paths rather than a single product. The rule
  [[Back Propagation]] is an efficient implementation of
- [[Differential]]: $dx$, $ds$, $d\mathbf{r}$, $dA$, $dV$, $dS$. Which element an integral carries
  is usually the hard half of setting it up

### Multivariable optimization

- [[Multivariable Optimization]]: critical points where $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$, and the Hessian
  test that sorts them into maxima, minima, and the case with no one-variable analogue, the saddle
- [[Lagrange Multipliers]]: optimising subject to a constraint, from the one geometric fact that a
  gradient is perpendicular to level curves. The multiplier is a rate of change, not a bookkeeping
  device

### Vector calculus

- [[Vector Calculus]]: the index for the block. Three operators, three kinds of integral, three
  theorems relating them
- [[Vector Field]]: a vector at every point. What [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]'s vectors become when they are
  allowed to vary from place to place
- [[Divergence]]: spreading, a scalar. Source, sink, or incompressible
- [[Curl]]: local rotation, a vector, computed as a cross-product [[Determinant]]
- [[Conservative Vector Field]]: the fields that are gradients. Path independence, potentials, and
  why a curl-free field on a domain with a hole can still fail to be one
- [[Parameterization]]: curves by one parameter, surfaces by two. Every integral below is evaluated
  by doing this first
- [[Line Integral]]: along a path. $\int_C f\,ds$ is [[Arc Length]] with a weight, and
  $\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$ is work and circulation
- [[Surface Integral]]: over a sheet. The same two kinds, one dimension up, with orientation now a
  choice that has to be kept
- [[Flux]]: what the vector surface integral measures, and the quantity [[Divergence]] is the
  density of
- [[Multiple Integration]]: triple integrals, order of integration and Fubini, and the Jacobian as
  the local volume-scaling factor
- [[Green's Theorem]]: circulation round a plane loop becomes curl over the region inside
- [[Stokes' Theorem]]: the same for a surface in space, so any two surfaces sharing a boundary give
  the same answer
- [[Divergence Theorem]]: flux out of a closed surface becomes divergence over the solid. The
  theorem that derives the [[Heat Equation]]

### Ordinary differential equations

- [[Differential Equations]]: the index. How to classify an equation (order, linearity,
  homogeneity, coefficients) and the table mapping each class to its method
- [[Homogeneous ODE]]: constant coefficients, characteristic equation, and the three root cases.
  Complex roots are what oscillation is
- [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]]: complementary plus particular, the same structure theorem as
  $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$
- [[Undetermined Coefficients]]: guess the shape of the forcing term, match coefficients, and
  multiply by $t$ when the guess collides with the complementary solution
- [[Cauchy-Euler]]: the variable-coefficient family that still solves in closed form, because
  $x^ky^{(k)}$ is scale invariant
- [[Systems of Differential Equations]]: coupled equations decoupled by
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]. The [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] payoff, and the largest idea in the block
- [[Phase Portrait]]: stability read off the eigenvalues, without solving anything
- [[Series Solutions]]: power series near ordinary and regular singular points, when nothing else
  works

### Convergence, revisited

This block adds no notes, on purpose. The sequence and series machinery belongs to [[CALCULUS 2]]
and is used here rather than rebuilt: [[Sequence]], [[Infinite Series]], [[Convergence Tests]],
[[Power Series]], and [[Taylor Series]]. What this course adds is the reason to care, which is that
a [[Series Solutions|series solution]] is worthless outside its radius of convergence and a mode
expansion of a [[Partial Differential Equations|PDE]] is an infinite sum whose convergence is the
question of whether the model means anything at its boundary.

### Partial differential equations

- [[Partial Differential Equations]]: several independent variables, so arbitrary functions rather
  than arbitrary constants, and separation of variables as the one method
- [[Heat Equation]]: diffusion. Smooths everything, cannot be run backwards
- [[Wave Equation]]: propagation. Shapes travel at speed $c$ and nothing is lost
- [[Laplace's Equation]]: steady state. Harmonic functions, the mean value property, and extrema
  only on the boundary

## Core Facts to Know

- A [[Partial Derivative]] is an ordinary derivative with the other variables treated as constants.
  **Clairaut**: if the mixed partials are continuous, $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$.
- $\nabla f$ points along **steepest ascent**, $\lVert\nabla f\rVert$ is how steep, and $\nabla f$
  is **perpendicular to level sets**. The directional derivative is $D_{\mathbf{u}}f = \nabla f\cdot\mathbf{u}$
  for a unit $\mathbf{u}$.
- Multivariable chain rule: **one term per path** through the dependency tree, each term a product
  along that path. Left side is $d$ if one independent variable remains, $\partial$ if more than one.
- Critical points solve $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$. With $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2$: $D>0$ and
  $f_{xx}>0$ is a minimum, $D>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$ a maximum, **$D<0$ a saddle**, $D=0$ no information.
- Constrained optimisation: $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$ with $g = k$. The multiplier is
  $df^*/dk$, the rate the optimum improves as the constraint loosens.
- The three operators by shape: $\nabla f$ scalar to vector, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}$ vector to
  scalar, $\nabla\times\mathbf{F}$ vector to vector. Checking the shape catches most errors before
  any arithmetic.
- $\nabla\times(\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}$ and $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0$. Both follow
  from equality of mixed partials.
- **Divergence is flux per unit volume; curl is circulation per unit area.** Every big theorem in
  the course is that sentence integrated.
- A field is conservative iff it is a gradient iff line integrals are path independent iff every
  closed-loop integral is zero iff its curl vanishes, **and the last equivalence needs a simply
  connected domain**. $\langle -y, x\rangle/(x^2+y^2)$ is the counterexample when it does not.
- $\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$ flips sign when the orientation reverses; $\int_C f\,ds$ does
  not. Same distinction for surfaces, where the normal picks the side.
- $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$ with $C$ **counterclockwise**. The area of a
  region is $\oint_C x\,dy$, which is the special case $P=0$, $Q=x$.
- Stokes: $\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}$.
  The right side depends only on the boundary, **so the surface may be swapped for a convenient one**.
- Divergence theorem: $\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F})\,dV$,
  outward normal, closed surface only.
- Volume elements: $r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$ cylindrical, $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$
  spherical. The extra factor is the **Jacobian**, a [[Determinant]], and it is there because
  changing coordinates stretches volume.
- Triple integral limits are read inside out: the innermost may depend on both outer variables, the
  outermost must be constants. Fubini permits reordering, and one of the six orders is usually much
  easier than the rest.
- $ay''+by'+cy=0$ has solutions decided by the roots of $ar^2+br+c=0$: distinct real gives
  $c_1e^{r_1t}+c_2e^{r_2t}$, **repeated gives $c_1e^{rt}+c_2te^{rt}$**, complex $\alpha\pm\beta i$
  gives $e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t + c_2\sin\beta t)$.
- Non-homogeneous solutions are $y = y_c + y_p$, and the **initial conditions are applied to the
  sum**, never to $y_c$ alone. Same structure as one particular solution plus the null space of a
  matrix.
- In [[Undetermined Coefficients]], use the **full** polynomial and **both** sine and cosine, and
  multiply by $t$ when a guessed term already appears in $y_c$. That collision is resonance.
- For $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, each eigenpair gives $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ and the general
  solution is their linear combination. **Stability is exactly "every eigenvalue has negative real
  part"**; complex eigenvalues spiral, opposite real signs give a saddle.
- A PDE's general solution carries arbitrary **functions**, not constants. Separation of variables
  assumes $u = X(x)T(t)$ and turns one PDE into two ODEs, with boundary conditions selecting the
  modes and a [[Fourier Series]] fitting the initial data to them.
- $u_t = ku_{xx}$ diffuses and smooths, $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ propagates and conserves,
  $\nabla^2u = 0$ is the steady state of the first. **One extra time derivative is the entire
  difference between the first two.**
- Harmonic functions take their maximum and minimum **on the boundary**, and equal their own
  average over any circle.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200) and [[CALCULUS 2]] (MATH 2200) are the prerequisites, and the handoff
  is explicit in both directions. Calc 2 introduces [[Partial Derivative]], [[Gradient]],
  [[Multivariable Chain Rule]], and first and second order [[Differential Equations]] and hands all
  of them here; it keeps [[Double Integral]] (MRU teaches doubles there, triples here under
  [[Multiple Integration]]) and it keeps the convergence material outright. Every technique in
  [[Integration Techniques]] is a working prerequisite, because solving anything in this course ends
  in an integral.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) is the other prerequisite and the debt is larger than it looks.
  [[Vector]] and [[Dot Product]] are the algebra every operator here is written in,
  [[Determinant]] is both the [[Curl]] cross product and the Jacobian and the Hessian test,
  [[Vector Space]] and [[Linear Dependence]] are why "general solution" means a linear combination,
  and [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] with [[Diagonalization]] are the entire method of
  [[Systems of Differential Equations]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) arrives at this course's second-derivative test
  from the other side: definiteness of a [[Quadratic Form]] **is** the Hessian criterion, stated in
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] rather than in a determinant, and it is the version
  that survives past two variables. [[Principal Component Analysis]] is a
  [[Lagrange Multipliers]] problem in disguise.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) picks up where
  [[Partial Differential Equations|separation of variables]] stops. The modes it produces are
  [[Orthogonal Functions]], and writing an initial condition in that basis is a [[Fourier Series]]
  with [[Fourier Coefficients]] given by integrals.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and the neural network notes in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] run on this
  course. [[Gradient Descent]] is [[Multivariable Optimization]] without a closed form,
  [[Back Propagation]] is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] with a very large dependency tree,
  [[Loss Function]] is the $f$ being minimised, and saddle points are a real obstacle rather than a
  curiosity.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): a joint or bivariate [[Probability Density Function]] is normalised
  by a double integral and its marginals are integrals over one variable, so
  [[Multiple Integration]] is what makes multivariate probability computable at all.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: every equation here is
  ultimately solved numerically, so the discretisation of [[Laplace's Equation]] is a large sparse
  [[System of Linear Equations]], and the error in it is bounded by the truncation of a
  [[Taylor Series]].
